(CNN) -- Robert Barnett, a prominent Washington attorney, has worked on eight national presidential campaigns, focusing on debate preparation. He played the role of George H.W. Bush in practice debates with Geraldine Ferraro in 1984 and with Michael Dukakis in 1988, and practice debated Bill Clinton more than 20 times during the 1992 campaign. He also played the role of Dick Cheney in 2000 and 2004 and helped prepare Hillary Clinton for 23 primary debates for the 2008 nomination. Barnett spoke with CNNI's Michael Holmes. Robert Barnett has been in practice debates with Democrats from Geraldine Ferraro to Bill Clinton. CNN: How does Tuesday night's town hall format differ from other debates? Barnett: The individuals will not necessarily express the question as a journalist would. So, for example, one of these people will probably not ask about Internal Revenue Service Code section 341, but rather will ask about their taxes and their tax burdens and what they care about with respect to taxation. And so you have to be very careful to be sure you understand what the individual is asking about and you have to be particularly careful to answer the question, because if you don't, you risk alienating the questioner and the audience and the listeners. CNN: You're in a unique position. You have prepped, I think, seven or eight presidential campaigns. You've done debate prep, you've stood in and played the role of Dick Cheney and others. What's that like? What are you trying to do to prepare the candidate, any candidate? Barnett:  If I'm playing the surrogate, if you will, if I'm the Republican for a Democrat, I try to prepare myself -- not to imitate; I'm not Darrell Hammond or Dana Carvey. I'm not that talented. But I try to be ready with what my candidate that I'm playing, if you will, has said -- the exact words used, the way they counterattack, the way they attack. And I try to make sure that the candidate I'm working with, meaning the Democrat, has heard just about everything that they could hear from their opponent before they ever walk on the stage. CNN: Do you try to bait them, get them to bite a little and then say that's not what you should be doing? Barnett: Well, it can get pretty contested. When I prepared with Rep. Geraldine Ferraro in 1984 when she was running against then-vice president George Herbert Walker Bush, I baited her a lot and she got so angry with me that she frequently walked over to me and slugged me on the arm. So I left the process black and blue. CNN: When you're doing that sort of thing, how direct can you be with the candidate? Or do you have to treat them with a bit of kid gloves? Barnett: I treat them with no kid gloves. It's fair to say I'm direct, I make sure they hear everything from me before they hear it on the stage and maybe hear it even a little more aggressively so they can be prepared.

**[CNN TRANSCRIPT]**

**PROGRAM:** CNN Newsroom  
**ANCHOR:** Michael Holmes  
**GUEST:** Robert Barnett (Washington Lawyer & Democratic Debate Prep Veteran)  

---

**MICHAEL HOLMES, CNN ANCHOR:** Welcome back. As the presidential campaign swings into high gear, both campaigns are locking themselves away in hotel conference rooms for what is arguably the most intense phase of any campaign: debate prep. 

Few people understand the high-stakes theater of these preparations better than Washington super-lawyer Bob Barnett. Over the last three decades, he has helped prepare Democratic presidential and vice-presidential candidates for more than ten debate cycles. But he isn’t just an advisor—he is famous for playing the role of the Republican opponent in mock debates. He’s been George H.W. Bush, Dick Cheney, Sarah Palin, and Newt Gingrich, just to name a few. 

Bob Barnett joins me now from Washington. Bob, great to have you with us. 

**ROBERT BARNETT:** Great to be with you, Michael.

**HOLMES:** Now, Bob, when you step into a room to play someone like George H.W. Bush opposite Bill Clinton in 1992, or Dick Cheney opposite John Edwards in 2004—how do you prepare? Are you doing an impression, or is it purely strategic?

**BARNETT:** *[Laughs]* Well, Michael, I always tell people: I’m not an actor. I don’t do Saturday Night Live impressions. If you’re trying to do a voice or a caricature, you’re missing the point. 

My job when I played George H.W. Bush or Dick Cheney was to *think* like them, to master their record, to anticipate their lines of attack, and to deliver their arguments with total conviction. You watch hours of tape. You learn their mannerisms, their tells, what makes them angry, and how they react under pressure. The goal is to make the mock debate so tough, so realistic, that when your candidate walks onto the actual stage, nothing the real opponent says comes as a surprise.

**HOLMES:** Let’s talk about Dick Cheney in 2004. He was known as a formidable, unflappable debater. How did you embody that specific persona for John Edwards?

**BARNETT:** Cheney was unique because his power came from his calm, authoritative quietness. He didn't raise his voice; he projected gravitas. So when I prepped John Edwards, I didn't try to out-shout him. I sat back, used a very measured tone, and hit him with heavy policy experience. I wanted John to get used to confronting someone who wouldn't be baited into a shouting match, but who would relentlessly undermine his readiness to be commander-in-chief. You have to give your candidate the exact flavor of the challenge they’re about to face.

**HOLMES:** One of the most tricky debate formats for candidates is the town hall style. You were right there in 1992 when the town hall format was first introduced in Richmond, Virginia—Bill Clinton, George H.W. Bush, and Ross Perot. What makes the town hall format so fundamentally different from a traditional podium debate?

**BARNETT:** The town hall is entirely a test of empathy and connection. At a podium, you’re talking to the moderator or directly into the camera to the audience at home. In a town hall, you are talking to an undecided voter standing six feet away from you, holding a microphone. 

If you give a canned, political speech to a citizen who just asked you how high milk prices are affecting your family, you lose. You have to listen, you have to validate their concern, and you have to answer *them*—not just the television audience. 

**HOLMES:** And physical movement plays a huge role in town halls, doesn't it? 

**BARNETT:** Crucial. In a podium debate, you're locked in place. In a town hall, the stage is open. How you walk, how close you get to the questioner, your body language when the *other* candidate is speaking—it’s all being watched. 

Back in 1992, President George H.W. Bush famously looked at his watch during the town hall. It was a split-second gesture, but to the audience, it signaled that he was bored or had somewhere better to be. Meanwhile, Bill Clinton walked right up to the edge of the stage, looked the questioner in the eye, and asked her how the recession had affected *her*. That contrast defined the debate, and frankly, it changed the trajectory of that election.

**HOLMES:** When you prep a candidate for a town hall, how do you simulate that unpredictable element of citizen questions?

**BARNETT:** We bring in a group of staffers or outside volunteers who play the "voters." We don't let the candidate know what questions are coming. We tell the mock voters to ask tough, personal, sometimes bizarre questions—because that's what happens in real life. We train the candidate to abandon the binder, get out from behind the script, and connect on a human level. 

**HOLMES:** Is it hard for high-profile politicians—who are used to being the most powerful person in the room—to take brutal feedback from you during these mock sessions?

**BARNETT:** It takes a very disciplined candidate to endure debate prep. You are standing in a room with your closest advisors, and someone like me is attacking you, exposing your weaknesses, telling you your answers are too long, or that your body language looks defensive. It's uncomfortable. But the best candidates—like Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, Joe Biden—they welcome it because they know the stakes on debate night are absolute.

**HOLMES:** In your view, Bob, what is the ultimate goal of debate prep? Is it to land a knockout punch, or to avoid a fatal mistake?

**BARNETT:** Knockout punches are rare, Michael. The real goal is consistency, authenticity, and executing your strategy. If you leave the stage having clearly communicated to the American people who you are, what you stand for, and why the other person shouldn't have the job, you’ve had a good night. 

**HOLMES:** Fascinating behind-the-scenes insight. Bob Barnett, Washington attorney and veteran of many a debate battle room—thank you so much for joining us.

**BARNETT:** Thanks for having me, Michael. Always a pleasure.

**ROBERT BARNETT:** It is an exhaustive process. When I was tasked with playing George H.W. Bush for Geraldine Ferraro in 1984, and later for Michael Dukakis and Bill Clinton, I spent weeks studying him. I watched hundreds of hours of video footage. I didn't just study his policies; I studied his speech patterns, his hand gestures, his nervous tics, his favorite phrases, and his debate tactics. 

If your candidate is going to be attacked on the real stage, they cannot be hearing the line or seeing the gesture for the first time. My job as the sparring partner was to make the rehearsal far harder, far more brutal, and far nastier than the actual night would ever be.

**JANE MORAN:** How do you get into character? Do you stay in character during the rehearsals?

**ROBERT BARNETT:** Absolutely. The moment the timer starts, I am no longer Bob Barnett, friendly DC lawyer. I am the opponent. I would wear the kind of suit they wore. I would adopt their tone. 

When I played Dick Cheney against John Edwards in 2004, Cheney had a very specific, calm, almost stern, authoritative delivery. I had to master that low, steady voice that made even aggressive attacks sound like common sense. 

And you have to know how to press your candidate’s buttons. Everyone has a trigger—a policy topic that makes them defensive, or a personal slight that makes them angry. In a mock debate, my sole objective was to try and make our candidate lose their cool. If they blew up at me in a hotel conference room, we could fix it. If they blew up on live television to 70 million people, we were sunk.

**JANE MORAN:** Is it uncomfortable to stand opposite a friend—someone who might be the next President of the United States—and relentlessly attack them?

**ROBERT BARNETT:** It’s deeply uncomfortable at first. You’re slinging insults and harsh political attacks at someone you respect, sometimes feet away from their spouse or top advisors sitting in the front row. 

I remember times where I would deliver a particularly nasty line during a mock debate, and the room would just go dead silent. But the candidates understand the rules of the game. Bill Clinton, for instance, loved the sparring. If I hit him with a tough line, you could see his eyes light up—he wanted to figure out how to counter-punch immediately.

**JANE MORAN:** What is the biggest mistake a candidate can make in a town hall debate specifically?

**ROBERT BARNETT:** Forgetting who they are talking to. In a traditional debate, you are talking to your opponent or the moderator. In a town hall, if you spend all your time arguing with your opponent, the audience in the room feels ignored. 

The candidates who win town halls are the ones who make the voter asking the question feel like they are the only two people in the room. You have to answer the person, not just the policy.

**JANE MORAN:** Robert Barnett, veteran of the debate prep room, thank you so much for sharing your insights with us today.

**ROBERT BARNETT:** My pleasure, Jane.

**[SCENE END]**

---

### Key Takeaways from Mock Debate Prep:

1. **Environmental Simulation:** Camps erect replica stages down to the lighting and floor coverings to ensure muscle memory carries over to the actual broadcast.
2. **Psychological Conditioning:** Sparring partners deliberately use personal slights, low blows, and key policy traps to desensitize the candidate before the real event.
3. **The "Town Hall Trap":** Unlike podium debates focused on counter-punching the opponent, town halls reward candidates who prioritize the physical voter in the room over arguing with their rival.

**INSIDE THE WAR ROOM**

# ‘No Kid Gloves’: Political Insider Bob Barnett on the Brutal Art of Presidential Debate Prep

**By Julian Vance**  
*Published October 24, 2023*

For more than three decades, Washington super-lawyer Robert "Bob" Barnett has held a unique and terrifying position in American politics. As the Democratic Party’s premier debate surrogate, Barnett has played the role of the Republican adversary in ten presidential and vice-presidential prep cycles. He has transformed himself into George W. Bush, Dick Cheney, Sarah Palin, and Mitt Romney, spending hundreds of hours attacking candidates like Bill Clinton, Al Gore, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden.

With millions of voters watching, a single debate misstep can sink a presidential campaign. We sat down with Barnett to discuss his rigorous preparation methods, why he refuses to treat his own party's candidates with kid gloves, and the psychological labyrinth of the coveted town hall debate format.

***

**The Capital News:** *Bob, you’ve spent decades playing the antagonist in mock debates. When you take on the persona of a candidate’s rival, how do you actually prepare for that role?*

**Robert Barnett:** It’s a full-immersion exercise. I don’t just read policy papers; I study hundreds of hours of video footage. I want to know their rhetorical crutches, their vocal inflections, their favorite pivot phrases, and their body language when they get angry. 

When I played George W. Bush for Al Gore in 2000, or Sarah Palin for Joe Biden in 2008, my goal wasn't to caricature them—it was to embody their most effective, dangerous political selves. You have to give your candidate the most formidable version of their opponent. If you give them a weak imitation in practice, you are setting them up for failure on live television.

**The Capital News:** *You are famous for being utterly ruthless in these mock debates. Why is it so crucial not to pull punches, even when sparring with a future President of the United States?*

**Barnett:** Because the opponent won’t pull punches, and neither will the moderators. 

Candidates spend their days surrounded by staff, donors, and voters who tell them how brilliant they are. They live in a bubble of affirmation. My room is the place where that bubble gets popped. I attack their record, their character, their family’s business dealings, their age—whatever the opponent is going to hit them with. 

If a candidate is going to get flustered, angry, or freeze up, I want it to happen in a carpeted hotel conference room in front of twelve staff members, not in front of 70 million voters. My rule is simple: treat them with zero kid gloves. If the candidate leaves the mock debate room hating me a little bit, then I’ve done my job.

```
       "If a candidate is going to get flustered, angry, or freeze up, 
       I want it to happen in a carpeted hotel conference room in front 
       of twelve staff members, not in front of 70 million voters."
                                  — Robert Barnett
```

**The Capital News:** *Can you walk us through the physical setup of these sparring sessions? How far do you go to recreate the real environment?*

**Barnett:** We replicate everything to the exact inch. If the real debate has 40-inch lecterns, we build 40-inch lecterns. If the temperature in the hall is going to be set to 65 degrees, we crank the air conditioning down. We hire professional camera crews, set up red timing lights, and invite a small audience of staffers to act as the crowd. 

We even replicate the lighting so the candidate gets used to the glare and heat. The goal is to eliminate any potential environmental shock on debate night. By the time the candidate walks onto the actual stage, their brain should feel like it’s just step ten of a process they’ve already done nine times.

**The Capital News:** *Let’s talk about formats. The town hall debate is often considered the most unpredictable format. What makes it so complex compared to a traditional podium debate?*

**Barnett:** The town hall isn't a debate; it’s a physical play. In a podium debate, you are anchored. You look at the moderator or the camera. In a town hall, you are roaming a stage with a hand-held microphone, surrounded by undecided voters. The mechanics are entirely different.

First, your posture and spatial awareness are critical. You have to know where the cameras are at all times, but more importantly, you have to engage directly with the citizen asking the question. If a voter asks about prescription drug costs because their daughter is sick, you don't look at your opponent, and you don't look at the moderator. You walk up to that voter, make eye contact, and speak to their pain.

**The Capital News:** *What are the fatal traps candidates fall into during a town hall?*

**Barnett:** The biggest mistake is forgetting that you are always on camera, even when you aren't speaking. In 1992, George H.W. Bush famously looked at his watch during a town hall question. It signaled to the audience that he was bored and wanted it to be over. It was fatal. 

Another trap is invading the other candidate’s physical space aggressively, or conversely, looking intimidated when they invade yours. You have to master the optics of non-verbal telemetry. How do you stand when the other person is talking? Do you look attentive, dismissive, or anxious? 

In prep, we train candidates on "active listening." If the opponent is making a point, you don't scowl or shake your head frantically—that makes you look weak. You take notes, maintain a neutral demeanor, and wait for your turn. 

**The Capital News:** *If you could give a candidate just one golden rule for debate night, what would it be?*

**Barnett:** Win the opening twenty minutes, and never take the bait. 

Viewers decide very early on who looks presidential and who looks defensive. Your opponent’s primary goal is to bait you into defending your weaknesses rather than talking about your vision. The moment you start spending your time answering their accusations, you are playing on their home field. A great debater acknowledges the swing, pivots seamlessly, and puts the focus right back on the choice facing the American people.
